text.p: The pound was narrowly off session highs in late Europe but remained in fine spirits after strong new UK data catapulted it out of early morning doldrums.
October unemployment fell 40,800 versus the forecast 25,000 drop, September wage costs rose 5.2 percent against the 4.5 predicted, and average earnings grew 4.0 percent, as expected.
"It does make the case for a rate rise that much clearer," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Newly-released minutes showed Bank of England governor Eddie George argued at the October 23 UK monetary meeting that interest rates might have to rise above six percent.
UK base rates were held at 5.75 percent after that meeting, but were subsequently hiked to six percent on October 30.
"The data add ammunition for Eddie George to ask for higher rates," said Dharshini David, UK economist at HSBC Markets.

UK employment minister Eric Forth said October's large unemployment drop may have been exaggerated by a new jobless benefits system, the jobseekers allowance, but the underlying trend was still downwards.
David said other factors too, such as the fact that most of the growth in employment had been part-time, suggested the figures were weaker than they appeared at first glance.
"So there is room for Clarke to stay where he is -- as long as he comes in with a prudent budget he should be able to hang on (in resisting further tightening)," she said.
Analysts believe the advent of the next UK election -- which must be held by May -- reduces the likelihood that Chancellor Kenneth Clarke will sanction more tightening in the near term.
But if October retail price data out Thursday show the predicted rise in annual inflation, the odds on another pre-election rate rise will certainly shorten, they say.
RPI is seen falling 0.2 percent on the month but rising 2.5 percent on the year, up from September's 2.1 increase.
RPIX core inflation, which excludes mortgage interest payments, is seen edging up to 3.1 percent from 2.9 -- yet further from the government's target of 2.5 percent.
According to the September 23 minutes, Eddie George said the Bank of England was less confident that underlying inflation would fall to the target level.
But he said sterling's relative strength, if it persisted, would help contain any immediate pickup in inflation.
The pound put on a late spurt in Europe, rising to 2.4927/32 marks by 1519 GMT from 2.4743/53 in late Europe on Tuesday, and to $1.6560/70 from yesterday's close around $1.6475/85.
Technical analysts said cable would have difficulty breaching $1.6580, the site of its recent four-year high.
On a trade-weighted basis, the pound romped to 91.2 from its previous close here of 90.5.
